Thank you for your careful reading and detailed summary. Your suggestions on improving the paper presentation have helped us make our work better. In the paper revision, we have expanded __Appendix C__ with a thorough introduction to the definition of and intuition behind intrinsic dimension. In addition, we add __Section 7__ in the main body to discuss limitations and further work of our study. We hope these additions provide enough intuition and background needed to understand the role of intrinsic dimension in our analysis. Below, we summarize the content in response to your questions.

> __1. Definition and intuition behind intrinsic dimension:__ 

In Appendix C, we include a clear conceptual explanation with concrete examples, a discussion of prior deep learning work involving intrinsic dimension, and a more detailed explanation of the 2-NN algorithm. To briefly walk through the concept, the intrinsic dimension of a dataset is the minimum number of independent parameters needed to describe the data without significant information loss. For example, a spiral curve in 10-dimensional space has an intrinsic dimension of 1 (specifying a single parameter, arc length, uniquely determines any points), even though the spiral has variance across all 10 dimensions. This illustrates that curved manifolds can have low intrinsic dimension despite high ambient dimensionality, which PCA-based methods cannot capture. In our formulation of regression problems, ID_Y​ measures the geometric complexity of targets, while ID_H​ measures the complexity of learned features. The relationship between these quantities determines whether models are over-compressed (ID_H < ID_Y) or under-compressed (ID_H >> ID_Y), which can explain their generalization behavior. 

> __2. About understanding Figure 4:__

Figure 4 illustrates the relationship between two metrics for characterizing learned representations: Neural Regression Collapse (NRC1) and Intrinsic Dimension (ID_H). NRC1 measures the degree to which penultimate-layer features collapse into an n-dimensional linear subspace (where n is the target dimension). While NRC1 and ID_H​ show positive correlation in non-collapsed models with non-trivial NRC1 values, Figure 4 reveals a critical limitation of NRC1. In the collapsed regime (low or near-zero NRC1 values), models with nearly identical NRC1 exhibit widely varying ID_H​. For instance, in the Ant dataset (fifth panel), models at NRC1 ≈ 0 span ID_H from ~2 to ~5, and these models show substantially different test performance. This vertical spread demonstrates that NRC1, which only measures proximity to a linear subspace, cannot capture the nonlinear manifold structure within that subspace. 

ID_Y​ then provides an intuitive threshold. “ID_H < ID_Y”​ indicates over-compression. In contrast, NRC1 → 0 simply means features lie in an n-dimensional subspace, but provides no criterion for how much damage the collapse has inflicted on model generalization. Therefore, we made the main claim about Figure 4: “while the NRC1 metric is useful in understanding the linear-subspace structure of the last-layer features in collapsed models, it is inadequate at uncovering this more refined geometric structure."

> __3. Concerning limitations and future work of our study, Section 7 is added to address your concern. Below is a summary:__

Our study provides geometric insights into neural multivariate regression, but a full theoretical explanation linking intrinsic dimension and generalization remains incomplete. Also, the 2-NN estimator used in the experiments is reliable only for intrinsic dimensions below about 20, limiting its applicability in very high-dimensional settings. Last, current practical recommendations adjust intrinsic dimension indirectly through model regularizations, e.g., weight decay and dropout, since 2-NN intrinsic dimension estimate itself is not yet differentiable or directly optimizable. 

Future work includes developing theoretical generalization bounds involving intrinsic dimension, exploring alternative modeling frameworks beyond the unconstrained feature model (UFM), and creating differentiable or scalable intrinsic-dimension estimators that enable direct control over representation geometry during training. Further extending these ideas to generative modeling, reinforcement learning, multi-task learning, and other domains may yield a broader geometric understanding of deep learning systems.

We want to thank all reviewers for their efforts in writing reviews, constructive comments, and suggestions on improving our work. We have been working hard on augmenting the current work with both theoretical and empirical results in response to all questions and concerns. The revised manuscript has been uploaded with all changes and new content marked in blue. We would like to highlight some major modifications:
- In __Appendix F__ and __Section 6.1__, we answer in theory __why weight decay leads to collapse__ from the perspective of Unconstrained Feature Model (UFM).
- In __Appendix G__, we show that __dropout regularization and model depth__ can also effectively adjust ID_H. 
- In __Appendix H__, we experiment with __more tasks with varying sizes, increased ID_Y, and visual inputs__ to further support our empirical findings. 
- __Appendix H.1__ includes a concrete example in visual control tasks, demonstrating the __practical guideline of our work__.
- We create __Section 7__ in the main body, where we list __limitations and future work__ of our study.
- In __Appendix A__, we clarify the __notion of low-data tasks  and noisy target tasks__ discussed in Section 6.
- We have expanded __Appendix C__ with a thorough __introduction to the definition of and intuition behind intrinsic dimension__, together with more details about the 2-NN estimator.

We believe that these modifications have largely improved the paper quality and have enhanced the contribution of our study. We would appreciate it if the reviewers could take a look at the revisions. Should there be any further questions, we are happy to discuss and address them.

Thank you for your careful reading and detailed summary of our work. In the paper revision, we augment our study with additional theoretical analysis on why weight decay causes neural regression collapse in __Appendix F__; and with additional empirical analysis on factors (e.g., dropout and model depth) affecting the degree of collapse with zero or mild weight decay in __Appendix G__. Below, we summarize the new content in response to your comments

> 1. __“The paper lacks a more rigorous analysis.”__

We appreciate the reviewer's concern regarding the theoretical analysis. We agree that a complete theoretical characterization of the relationship between intrinsic dimension and generalization represents an important direction for future work.

Our work is primarily an empirical study that provides new geometric insights into neural multivariate regression through intrinsic dimension analysis. Within this scope, we have incorporated theoretical results to address key aspects of our findings:
- Why weight decay causes collapse: Using the Unconstrained Feature Model (UFM) framework, we prove in __Theorem 4 in Appendix F__ that weight decay fundamentally biases optimization toward collapsed solutions by forcing features into an n-dimensional subspace.

- Why collapsed models fail to generalize: Theorem 1 (Section 6.1) provides a geometric result from differential geometry showing that when ID_H < ID_Y​, the model cannot generate the full range of target data, leading to unavoidable reconstruction error.

While these results address important mechanistic questions raised by our empirical observations, we acknowledge that a more rigorous and complete theoretical treatment, such as deriving generalization bounds that incorporate intrinsic dimension, remains open and challenging. We have added a "Limitations and Future Work" section explicitly discussing this gap and outlining directions for future theoretical development.

We believe our empirical findings, combined with these theoretical insights, provide a valuable understanding of neural regression geometry and motivate further theoretical investigation by the community.

>  __2. “My understanding is that weight decay is not very often used in practice currently. Are there other interesting observations regarding neural collapse when weight decay is not used?”__

In Appendix G.1, we examine how dropout regularization affects both collapse and generalization in the absence of weight decay, for Hopper, Halfcheetah, and Ant datasets with both 1K and 20K samples. We argue that dropout regularization has been widely used across diverse deep learning domains up to now. Examples include, but are not limited to, language models [1], computer vision [2], reinforcement learning [3], and generative models [4]. Then, we observe that varying dropout values lead to the same conclusion made in the main body. 

1. Figure 13(a) and Figure 14(a) show the relationship between ID_H and NRC1. The results match the main observation from Figure 4, where we argue ID_H provides a more refined geometric structure than NRC1. 

2. Figure 13(b) and Figure 14(b) show the relationship between ID_H and test MSE. The results recover three regimes summarized in Table 2.

Interestingly, dropout regularization differs from weight decay in that mild dropout (e.g., $\leq 0.01$) can effectively increase both NRC1 and ID_H, preventing models from neural collapse. Therefore, it offers an alternative approach that can not only decrease but also increase the degree of model collapse. 

In Appendix G.2, we find that, with mild weight decay regularization (e.g., $\in [0.0001, 0.001]$), increasing model depth leads to smaller NRC1 and ID_H and thus to more collapsed features. 

In the end, we want to emphasize that weight decay is still commonly used across diverse deep learning domains, including:
-  regularizing transformer backbones for large language models and robotic generalist policies; 
- participating, by default, in the common Pytorch implementation of AdamW optimizer (default value = 0.01); 
- improving the sample efficiency of online reinforcement learning algorithms; 
- facilitating research in model plasticity in deep learning. 

We provide references supporting these at the beginning of Appendix G. Therefore, we believe that our study gives valuable practical insights on how to choose weight decay values efficiently to obtain the best training performance and feature embeddings across various deep learning domains.

__References:__

[1] Wolf et al., Transformers: State-of-the-Art Natural Language Processing (2020)

[2] Dosovitskiy et al., An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale (2021)

[3] Hiraoka et al., Dropout Q-Functions for Doubly Efficient Reinforcement Learning (2022)

[4] Tianhong Li and Kaiming He, Back to Basics: Let Denoising Generative Models Denoise (2025)

summary.value: This paper studies the geometric properties of neural multivariate regression. Based on the experiments on regression tasks, the submission explores the relations between the Neural Regression Collapse metric and the estimated intrinsic dimension via 2 nearest neighbors.

strengths.value:
1. It is interesting to investigate the geometric properties of neural multivariate regression.

2. The conclusion seems intuitive.

weaknesses.value:
1. From Figure 1, we observe the relations between the weight decay parameter and the collapse degree. What is the deeper explanation regarding this observation?

2. In the experiments, only two kinds of datasets with modest sizes are used. In order to draw a solid conclusion from experiments, it would be better to test more kinds of tasks with varying sizes.

3. The intrinsic dimensions of $Y$ in the experiments are small. It is interesting to explore if the same conclusion can be drawn from high dimensional situations.

4. It seems that the vision-based regression tasks are constructed on classification datasets. It is encouraging to test the regression vision tasks.

5. In general, the conclusion of the submission is intuitive. However, the deeper theoretical analysis is missing. 

6. The practical guideline is vague. How to increase or reduce the intrinsic dimension of the embeddings? In addition, the ideal $ID_H$ is related to $ID_Y$. However, it is difficult to accurately estimate $ID_Y$ in practice, making it challenging to determine if one should increase $ID_Y$ or not.

> __3. Concerning the practical guideline:__

We thank the reviewer for this question. We believe there may be a minor typo in the comment: in the final sentence, "determine if one should increase ID_Y​ or not" likely should read "determine if one should increase ID_H​ or not," since ID_Y​ (the intrinsic dimension of targets) is fixed for a given dataset while ID_H​ (the intrinsic dimension of last-layer features) is what we adjust through training choices. 

- Adjusting ID_H: In Figure 4, we have examined that increasing the weight decay value can lead to decreasing ID_H. In Appendix G, we provide two alternative approaches to adjust ID_H. Interestingly, dropout regularization differs from weight decay in that mild dropout (e.g., $\leq 0.01$) can effectively increase both NRC1 and ID_H, preventing models from neural collapse. Therefore, model dropout can not only decrease but also increase the degree of model collapse. In addition, Appendix G.2 shows that, with mild weight decay regularization (e.g., $\in [0.0001, 0.001]$), increasing model depth leads to smaller NRC1 and ID_H. We believe that a combination of these commonly used model regularizations can provide diverse strategies to adjust ID_H in the face of difficulties in real applications.

- Estimating ID_Y​: While the 2-NN estimator may be less reliable for intrinsic dimensions above 20, the target intrinsic dimension ID_Y​ is typically much lower for problems of practical interest. This assumption is rooted in the well-known manifold hypothesis [1]. In deep learning, it states that most high-dimensional real-world datasets actually lie on or close to low-dimensional manifolds embedded within the higher-dimensional input space. Recently, it has been verified and applied in empirical and theoretical findings among various deep learning domains, including reinforcement learning [2] and generative model training [3]. Thus, we believe that ID_Y​ can be estimated reliably and serves as a fixed reference point for diverse datasets across different domains.

- Practical guidelines: In Appendix H.1, we post a concrete example of the challenge for evaluating a control model in the real environment. Such a scenario matters, as policy evaluation is often expensive, unsafe, and risky for control tasks [4]. Validation MSE provides little indication of actual control performance in the real tasks. Practitioners must therefore rely on costly real-environment interactions to tune hyperparameters and assess the policy. In Figure 17, we show that the relationship between $ID_H$ and $ID_Y$ not only predicts test MSE but also aligns with the _true_ control performance obtained from environment interaction. In particular, the relationship between ID_H and normalized model performance exhibits the opposite `U-shape' behavior, achieving its best score when $ID_H \approx ID_Y$, mirroring the sweet-spot identified in Section 6.

Our findings provide actionable guidance for practitioners. By estimating ID_H​ and comparing it to ID_Y​, practitioners can diagnose whether their model is over-compressed or under-compressed. Our empirical analysis demonstrates how standard regularizations affect ID_H, allowing practitioners to adjust hyperparameters systematically based on the regime they are in, rather than relying on trial and error.

__References:__

[1] Charles et al., Testing the manifold hypothesis (2016)

[2] Tiwari et al., Geometry of Neural Reinforcement Learning in Continuous State and Action Spaces (2025)

[3] Tianhong Li and Kaiming He, Back to Basics: Let Denoising Generative Models Denoise (2025)

[4] Levine et al., Offline reinforcement learning: Tutorial, review, and perspectives on open problems (2020)

Thanks for your suggestions on improving our work from both theoretical and practical perspectives. In the paper revision, we augment our study with additional theoretical analysis on why weight decay causes neural regression collapse in __Appendix F__; and with additional empirical results for more tasks with varying sizes, increased ID_Y and visual inputs in __Appendix H__. Below, we summarize the new content in response to your comments.

> __1.  “What is the deeper explanation regarding the relations between the weight decay parameter and the collapse degree?” “The deeper theoretical analysis is missing.”__

We appreciate the reviewer's concern regarding the theoretical analysis. We agree that a complete theoretical characterization of the relationship between intrinsic dimension and generalization represents an important direction for future work.

Our work is primarily an empirical study that provides new geometric insights into neural multivariate regression through intrinsic dimension analysis. Within this scope, we have incorporated theoretical results to address key aspects of our findings:

- Why weight decay causes collapse: Using the Unconstrained Feature Model (UFM) framework, we prove in __Theorem 4 (Appendix F)__ that weight decay fundamentally biases optimization toward collapsed solutions by forcing features into an n-dimensional subspace.

- Why collapsed models fail to generalize: Theorem 1 (Section 6.1) provides a geometric result from differential geometry showing that when ID_H < ID_Y​, the model cannot generate the full range of target data, leading to unavoidable reconstruction error.

While these results address important mechanistic questions raised by our empirical observations, we acknowledge that a more rigorous and complete theoretical treatment, such as deriving generalization bounds that incorporate intrinsic dimension, remains open. We have added a "Limitations and Future Work" section explicitly discussing this gap and outlining directions for future theoretical development.

We believe our empirical findings, combined with these theoretical insights, provide a valuable understanding of neural regression geometry and motivate further theoretical investigation by the community.

> __2. In terms of experimenting with more tasks:__

In __Appendix H__, we add four more challenging tasks with varying sizes (up to 500K), increased ID_Y (up to 20), and visual inputs (two visual continuous control tasks). Among all new experiments, we confirm that our main findings in Sections 5 and 6 remain intact and inclusive:

1. ID_H provides a more refined geometric structure than NRC1. Collapsed models with near-zero NRC1 values have varying ID_H below or in the vicinity of ID_Y (< n), while non-collapsed models with non-trivial NRC1 maintain their ID_H to be above ID_Y and to be positively correlated with NRC1. 

2. The results recover three regimes summarized in Table 2 about the relationship between ID_H and model generalization.  Models over-compress features when ID_H < ID_Y and thus lead to increasing test MSE (and thus poor generalization). Then, for small datasets with 1K-50K samples, $ID_H \approx ID_Y$ identifies the sweet spot where test MSE tends to be the lowest and exhibits the `U-shape' plots. Finally, with more samples, $ID_H \gg ID_Y$ achieves the best generalization with under-compressed models. 

Notably, for the most challenging tasks, e.g., Relocate and Humanoid_walk,  which have a substantially higher ID_Y due to their complex high-dimensional dynamics, models trained with _zero_ weight decay initially exhibit neural regression collapse with ID_H < ID_Y. This explains their extremely large test MSE and its negative correlation with ID_H, which matches the over-compressed regime (ID_H < ID_Y).

We thank you for your careful reading and insightful review. Below, we respond to your comments. 

> __1. “ID_H and NRC1 highly correlate and measure the same phenomenon.”__

We agree that some correlation is expected and that the intuition behind ID_H < ID_Y is reasonable: we view this clarity as a strength of our approach. We would like to clarify two key distinctions that motivate our use of intrinsic dimension:

1. __ID captures finer geometric structure than NRC1.__ Figure 4 shows that in the collapsed regime, models with nearly identical NRC1 values exhibit widely varying ID_H. For instance, in Ant (fifth panel), models at NRC1 ≈ 0 span ID_H from ~2 to ~5. These models show substantially different test performance in Figure 10(q). This vertical spread indicates that NRC1, which measures proximity to a linear subspace, cannot capture the nonlinear manifold structure that determines generalization. ID reveals this critical geometric detail.

2. __ID provides an intuitive threshold; NRC1 does not.__ The threshold ID_Y allows direct assessment: ID_H < ID_Y indicates over-compression. In contrast, NRC1 → 0 simply means features lie in an n-dimensional subspace, but provides no principled criterion for when this is problematic due to overcompression. Without knowing ID_Y, we cannot determine from NRC1 alone whether a collapsed model will generalize well or poorly. 

The reviewer is correct that ID_H < ID_Y, causing issues, is intuitive. Our contribution is showing that ID provides both the geometric resolution and the interpretable threshold needed to diagnose when and why collapse degrades performance, which NRC1 cannot provide. This is emphasized in Section 5 as well: 

“These models have a wide range of ID_H values, but are often clustered on a nearly vertical line below ID_Y. So, although the NRC1 metric is useful in understanding the linear-subspace structure of the last-layer features in collapsed models, it is inadequate at uncovering this more refined geometric structure.”


> __2. “How are low-data tasks or noisy target tasks formulated? Intuition or clear definition?”__

__Low-data task formulation:__ We acknowledge that there is no absolute threshold for what constitutes "low-data" versus "high-data" in general. In our experiments, we define this distinction by training models on two dataset sizes: 1,000 samples versus 20,000 samples. Given the substantial 20× difference, we treat the 1K setting as low-data and the 20K setting as high-data. Thank you for this comment. 

In the low-data regime, the empirical distribution estimated from training samples deviates substantially from the true underlying distribution. This causes models to learn features that reflect sampling artifacts rather than generalizable structure, resulting in inflated ID_H that includes dimensions corresponding to sample-specific variations. We clarify this distinction in the revision in __Appendix A1__.  

__Noisy-target task formulation:__ Again, thank you for this comment. We define this operationally as tasks where targets contain information that causes models to learn patterns that do not generalize to unseen data. 

In our CIFAR-10 task (Section 4), we construct noisy targets by projecting ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 features to 10 dimensions. The ImageNet encoder captures fine-grained visual details optimized for ImageNet classification. However, these details vary between semantically similar CIFAR-10 images due to instance-specific characteristics (color, texture, rendering at 32×32 resolution). High-capacity models can fit these instance-specific target components during training, but the learned mappings do not transfer to test images with different instance-specific details. Such target components are what we refer to as “noise” in our experiments. We now provide this definition in __Appendix A2__. 

> __3. “The definition of ID_P is missing.”__

We thank the reviewer for this observation. In the revision, we have added an explicit definition of ID_P​ (intrinsic dimension of the output predictions) in the Introduction, where we introduce the other intrinsic dimension notations (ID_H​, ID_Y​, ID_X).

summary.value: The current paper studies neural collapse, i.e., the "degeneracy" of last layer features, for multi-variate regression. Previously, a similar phenomenon was studied for classification and it was shown that the last layer features tightly cluster around class centroids. The current paper studies the problem from the angle of intrinsic dimension (ID), and presents empirical results of models trained with regularized least squares loss (by weight decay). By varying the regularization strength, models of different capacity are obtained and they lead to different behavior on two neural collapse metrics, NRC1 and ID. The paper shows that ID is a better metric for regression, ID is reduced during training and decreases with depth. The paper discusses correlations between these metrics and model generation, and suggests the critical regime being $ID_H=ID_Y$, i.e., the ID of last layer features need to be at least the ID of targets.

strengths.value: The ideas are very intuitive and the empirical observations match the intuitions.

weaknesses.value: My main concern is that, while the findings are interesting and intuitive, the paper lacks more rigorous analysis. The only theorem of the paper states that a collapsed model can not fit the data well. But this does not answer why collapse happened, and why ID is reduced during training (and maybe at what speed). Compared with most cited work on neural collapse for classification (accepted at top ML venues), the current paper is somewhat lacking in theoretical depth.

summary.value:
This paper studies geometry of representations in neural multivariate regression. It proposes use of intrinsic dimension of a feature/target manifold in place of the dimension of the linear subspace contining the manifold. The main findings are that the relation between the intrinsic dimension $ID_H$ of the learned features and the intrinsic dimension $ID_Y$ of the targets delineates under-compression and over-compression regimes and that the over-compression degrades generalization performance.

Reviewers valued positively the intuitive nature of the argument and the empirical support for that. Some reviewers noted that theoretical analysis is insufficient. Upon my own reading of the revised version, I feel that the revision was mainly done in Appendices, and consequently, the problems with the main text mentioned by Reviewers tvV2, pAdA, and bPR8 remain, and even the flow of the main text is now less smooth than the initial version. I thus think that this paper would benefit much from thorough reorganization taking account of the review comments.

A unique aspect of deep multivariate regression is that the feature manifold should be affine congruent to the target manifold. Appendix F in the revised manuscript contains theoretical results on neural regression collapse (NRC) via the unconstrained feature model (UFM). Theorem 2, due to Andriopoulos et al. (2024), states that when $0<c<\lambda_n$ the optimal feature matrix $H_\lambda$ is affine congruent to the target matrix $Y$. This fact might be in conflict with the argument in this paper, as the latter states that the affine congruence may not be maintained. This apparent inconsistency should be resolved.

- Multiletter symbols such as $ID_H$ should be avoided because they might be misinterpreted as products such as $I$ times $D_H$.
- Figure 4 caption: A description of the dot dashed lines for $ID_X$ should be added.
- Theorem 1: I feel that this theorem is an "overkill," because we now work not with smooth $g$ but with affine $g$, and the statement is almost trivial for the latter.

summary.value: This paper focuses on neural collapse in neural multivariate regression. The neural collapse is defined by NRC1 metric which is measuring the remaining signal of the last layer features from the projection onto the top principal components.  In the experiments the authors observe that intrinsic dimension of the last layer features is smaller than the intrinsic dimension of the labels in collapsed models whereas in the non-collapsed models it is the other way around. They claim that poor perfromance is observed in collapsed models while the performance in non-collapsed models depend on the data quality and the dataset size. Authors also provide emprical suggestions on last layer dimension based on the intrinsic dimension of the last layer and data quality. This paper also suggests that this observation of collapsed models having poor generalization is completely the opposite observation of previous work on neural collapse in classification tasks.

strengths.value: First, this paper shows that there is an important correlation between the NRC1 metric and the intrinsic dimension as stated in the Fig.4. Even though this is very expected behavior, this phenomenon is analyzed in the regression problems for the first time as authors suggested. Moreover, the behaviour of the intrinsic dimension in different layers in the training process (Fig.5) is analyzed well. Especially, providing the relation between IDP vs IDY for different settings (collapsed and non-collapsed) is good. In addition, the results in Fig.6, are very clean and shows interesting results like U-shape in (b)(e)(h) which actually unlocks new questions regarding the intrinsic dimension of the last layer and the intrinsic dimension of the labels.

weaknesses.value:
I think the main weakness is that the paper states that NRC1 metric and the intrinsic dimension of the last layer (IDH) is highly correlated. However, as far as I understand, this is very expected. As the intrinsic dimension is something similar to effective-rank, even if it is not a linear metric. NRC1 directly calculates how much noise is remain if you remove the first principal components. So, as far as I understand, by their definitions, they should be measuring very similar concepts. So, their correlation provided in Fig.4 is not suprising at all. 
In addition, some of the conclusions are very expected and do not contribute to the field. For example, when ID_H < ID_Y, it is also expected that the final layer has no enough representative power to learn the labels.

2 - In the paper, it is stated that when ID_H >= ID_Y , the test error depends on noise and dataset richness. And Fig.6, (b,e,h) are given as examples of low-data tasks and noisy-target tasks, while (k,n,q) are given as examples of high-data tasks or low-noise tasks. How do you say these are low-data tasks or noisy target tasks ? Is it just intuition or is there a clear definition ?
 
3 - I might have missed but I did not see the definition of ID_P in the paper even though it can be understood in the analysis of Fig.5, it is good to provide a definition.

summary.value: The paper examines the geometry of representations in neural multivariate regression and investigates why neural collapse—beneficial in classification—often degrades regression performance. It begins with the Neural Regression Collapse (NRC1) metric, which quantifies how tightly last-layer features concentrate in an $n$-dimensional linear subspace ($n$ here is the number of targets in multivariate regression). Although low NRC1 correlates with higher test error, the paper shows that NRC1 is limited because it captures only linear collapse and misses non-linear reductions in representational degrees of freedom. To address this, the authors estimate the intrinsic dimension $ID_H$ of the learned features and compare it with that of the targets $ID_Y$. They find that collapsed models satisfy $ID_H < ID_Y\, $ , indicating over-compression and poor generalization, while non-collapsed models maintain $ID_H \ge ID_Y$. The study thus argues that the intrinsic dimension provides a more faithful geometric measure than NRC1 for understanding regression generalization.

strengths.value:
Well-executed and engaging study: I enjoyed reading this paper. It presents a careful and comprehensive empirical investigation of representation geometry in neural multioutput regression, combining the NRC1 metric with intrinsic dimension analysis across diverse tasks. The experiments are clearly presented, and the findings—linking over-compression $ID_H < ID_Y$ to poor generalization—are convincing and well-supported.

See the summary.

weaknesses.value: I do not see any major weaknesses in the study itself. I have minor issues with the presentation. Especially, the intrinsic dimension should be part of the main text, with enough intuition. Based on the current version, I was not sure what I was supposed to think when I was trying to understand Figure 4. Perhaps this quantity is standard, but I am not familiar with it, and since it constitutes a significant part of the study, it should have been introduced more thoroughly.
